claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions.
Lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr stabilizes nanoscale modified grain-boundary regions.
The modified grain-boundary regions enhance dislocation mobility.
The modified grain-boundary regions blunt crack propagation.
WTaTiVZr is composed of equimolar refractory, relatively low-activation elements.
Using identical thermomechanical processing for WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten will control for grain size and microstructure.
Solid-solution formation in WTaTiVZr produces significant lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion creates localized stress fields that facilitate dislocation glide.
Lattice distortion facilitates grain-boundary sliding in WTaTiVZr.
Lattice distortion encourages stable nanoscale segregation at WTaTiVZr grain boundaries.
Stable nanoscale grain-boundary segregation suppresses crack nucleation and growth.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher elongation to failure than pure tungsten at 800–1200 °C under the proposed test conditions.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher critical stress-intensity factor than pure tungsten under the proposed test conditions.
Deformed WTaTiVZr will show greater dislocation mobility and modified grain-boundary phases that impede crack propagation.
Commercially pure tungsten exhibits limited plastic deformation at elevated temperatures.
Commercially pure tungsten has inherently low toughness at elevated temperatures.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate in controlled-grain-size, equiaxed microstructures between 800 and 1200 °C.
Significant segregation or formation of nonequilibrium phases may limit the applicability of the proposed mechanism.
